subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In composition, what does the 'rule of thirds' involve?
options: Using only three colours in an image
Dividing the frame into a 3x3 grid and placing key elements along the lines or intersections
Taking exactly three photographs of every subject
Cropping every image into three equal strips
questions.explain: The rule of thirds places points of interest on the gridlines or their intersections to create a balanced, engaging composition.

questions.q: Which camera setting controls the size of the lens opening and therefore how much light enters?
options: ISO
Aperture
White balance
Focal length
questions.explain: Aperture, measured in f-stops, controls the size of the lens opening and affects both exposure and depth of field.

questions.q: On a camera, what does the ISO setting primarily control?
options: The lens's zoom range
The sensor's sensitivity to light
The colour temperature of the image
The physical size of the print
questions.explain: A higher ISO increases the sensor's sensitivity to light, allowing shooting in darker conditions but often adding grain or noise.

questions.q: Why does using a wide aperture such as f/2.8 typically produce a blurred background?
options: It lengthens the shutter speed
It creates a shallow depth of field, keeping only the subject in focus
It increases the ISO automatically
It converts the image to black and white
questions.explain: A wide aperture (small f-number) gives a shallow depth of field, so the subject is sharp while the background falls out of focus.

questions.q: What is the main effect of using a slow shutter speed when photographing a moving subject?
options: The subject is frozen perfectly sharp
The image shows motion blur
The colours become more saturated
The depth of field increases
questions.explain: A slow shutter speed keeps the sensor exposed for longer, so moving subjects record as blur, conveying a sense of movement.

questions.q: How do 'leading lines' function within a composition?
options: They add text captions to the image
They guide the viewer's eye towards the main subject or focal point
They measure the correct exposure
They set the white balance
questions.explain: Leading lines are compositional lines that direct the viewer's gaze through the frame towards a focal point.

questions.q: Why might a photographer choose a low viewpoint (shooting from below) for a portrait?
options: To make the subject appear more imposing or powerful
To reduce the file size of the image
To automatically sharpen the background
To remove the need for editing
questions.explain: A low camera angle looks up at the subject, which tends to make them appear larger, dominant or more powerful.

questions.q: You want to freeze a fast-moving athlete so they appear perfectly sharp. Which setting change is most appropriate?
options: Use a much faster shutter speed
Use a much slower shutter speed
Use the lowest possible ISO
Use the narrowest aperture
questions.explain: A fast shutter speed exposes the sensor for a very short time, freezing rapid motion sharply.

questions.q: You are shooting indoors in low light and cannot use flash or a tripod. Which adjustment best helps you avoid a dark, blurred image?
options: Lower the ISO to its minimum
Raise the ISO to increase sensitivity
Narrow the aperture to f/22
Switch to a very slow shutter speed
questions.explain: Increasing the ISO makes the sensor more sensitive to light, allowing a usable exposure in dim conditions without flash or a tripod.

questions.q: What is the 'golden hour' in photography?
options: The period around midday when light is brightest
The hour after sunrise or before sunset when light is warm and soft
The time it takes to edit a photograph
The hour when a camera battery lasts longest
questions.explain: The golden hour occurs shortly after sunrise or before sunset, giving warm, soft, directional light favoured for portraits and landscapes.

questions.q: In a classic studio setup, what are the three lights of 'three-point lighting'?
options: Key light, fill light and back light
Flash, spotlight and torch
Red, green and blue lights
Front, top and floor lights
questions.explain: Three-point lighting uses a main key light, a fill light to soften shadows, and a back light to separate the subject from the background.

questions.q: What does the term 'chiaroscuro' describe in an image?
options: A soft, even, low-contrast lighting
A strong contrast between light and dark areas
A blurred, out-of-focus background
A colourful, saturated palette
questions.explain: Chiaroscuro refers to a dramatic contrast between bright light and deep shadow to create depth and mood.

questions.q: What happens when a subject is strongly lit from behind (backlighting) with little light on the front?
options: The subject appears as a silhouette
The subject becomes brightly and evenly lit
The background turns completely black
The image loses all contrast
questions.explain: Backlighting places the light source behind the subject, so the front is in shadow and the subject reads as a dark silhouette.

questions.q: In editing, what does adjusting the 'contrast' of an image do?
options: Changes the difference between the lightest and darkest tones
Rotates the image 90 degrees
Adds a border around the photograph
Changes the file format only
questions.explain: Increasing contrast widens the tonal difference between highlights and shadows; decreasing it makes tones more similar and flatter.

questions.q: Why might a photographer crop an image during editing?
options: To increase the camera's ISO
To improve the composition by removing distractions or reframing the subject
To add more pixels to the file
To change the shutter speed retrospectively
questions.explain: Cropping trims the edges of an image to tidy the composition, remove distractions or emphasise the subject.

questions.q: You want to create a dramatic silhouette of a person against a sunset. Where should the main light source be?
options: Directly in front of the person's face
Behind the person, facing the camera
Coming from directly above
Bounced off a white reflector at the front
questions.explain: Placing the bright light behind the subject leaves the front in shadow, producing a silhouette against the sky.

questions.q: Ansel Adams is best known for which genre of photography?
options: Fashion photography
Black-and-white landscape photography
Sports photography
Macro insect photography
questions.explain: Ansel Adams is celebrated for his dramatic black-and-white landscapes of the American West, such as Yosemite.

questions.q: Henri Cartier-Bresson is associated with which key photographic idea?
options: The 'decisive moment'
The 'rule of colour'
The 'zone of silence'
The 'golden ratio crop'
questions.explain: Cartier-Bresson, a pioneer of street photography, coined the 'decisive moment' — capturing a scene at its most telling instant.

questions.q: Cindy Sherman's work is best described as which of the following?
options: Wildlife photographs taken in the field
Staged self-portraits in which she adopts different characters
Aerial landscape photography
Sports action photography
questions.explain: Cindy Sherman constructs staged self-portraits, using costume and setting to play a range of characters and question identity.

questions.q: A student wants to explore documentary photography for a project. Which approach best fits this genre?
options: Recording real people and events to tell a truthful story about a situation
Digitally combining fantasy creatures into imaginary landscapes
Photographing only carefully arranged studio still lifes
Shooting abstract close-ups with no recognisable subject
questions.explain: Documentary photography captures real people, places and events to inform and tell an authentic story about the world.
